title: Protein–Single-Walled Carbon Nanotube Interfaces:  An Exploratory Docking and Molecular Dynamics Study
content:
A Carbon nanotube (CNTs) offers significant potential for biomedical applications due to their high affinity for proteins, carbohydrates, and lipids. Despite current limitations regarding size-dependent toxicity, they remain promising materials for biomolecule detection and targeted drug delivery. We use dockings to identify initial binding poses between SWCNTs—both functionalized (COOH/COO) and unfunctionalized—and four distinct proteins: Sambucus nigra Agglutinin II (SNA-II), Concanavalin A (Con-A), Bo-vine Serum Albumin (BSA), and Rice Beta-Glucosidase (RBG). We ran 50 ns molecular dynamics simulations with AMBER24 with three replicas each one. Finally, we calculated binding energies using MMPBSA. Dockings give a good starting pose, but MMP-BSA shows higher binding energies. Molecular dynamics show that the predicted binding regions by docking, stayed stable during simulations. CNTs bind away from the proteins' active sites. For glycosylated proteins, sugar groups are critical for binding, acting as main anchors for the CNT.
Simulations may reliably predict how proteins orient and bind to carbon nanotubes, showing that biologically important sites remain intact, this approach could help to screen nanomedicines and biosensors before lab testing. In addition, we observed pi-pi stacking between carbon rings, corroborating that in at least two proteins they are responsible for the CNT-protein interaction.
